newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vranitzky makes Albania ultimatum, PM holds talks. [CORRECTED 22:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky makes Albania ultimatum, PM holds talks. [CORRECTED 22:20 GMT]

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino planned to hold (corrects from "was in") late-night talks with his government on Tuesday as European envoy Franz Vranitzky warned the country's fate hinged on a political crisis being solved by the end of the day.
Vranitzky said time was running out for Albania after Fino failed to solve a deepening crisis over planned elections, which the premier said could have "unforeseen consequences".
Most political parties are threatening to boycott the poll over election rules they say are biased in favour of President Sali Berisha and his former ruling Democratic Party.
As Vranitzky's ultimatum deadline approached, Fino's office said the prime minister had had a meeting with Berisha and that the president had agreed to some amendments to the election rules.

Fino later went into a meeting with his nine-party national unity government, although it was not known whether there would be any breakthrough at the talks to convince the government parties to take part in the vote.
Amid intense Western concern, Italy and Greece added their voices to the chorus of warnings from governments.

"Time is running out. The government of national reconciliation, the prime minister and the president must reach agreement today," Vranitzky said in a statement after talks in Vienna on Albania with U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan.
Fino is trying to convince most political parties to take part in the vote, which Albania desperately needs to be seen as free and fair to stop it plunging back into violence.
Albania is still tense after a wave of riots and looting in February and March when thousands of people lost their money in the collapse of crooked pyramid investment schemes.

"Albania's prospects for the future and its place within the international community hinge on its ability to implement its commitments," said Vranitzy, a special envoy for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
Vranitzky has made five fruitless trips to Albania since the unrest began and rumours abound he will return this week.
An OSCE official said Vranitzky meant that if compromise was not found for the elections then assistance from the OSCE and other organisations may be withdrawn.
Annan also urged agreement after the talks.
"The parties must understand that they have to strike a compromise in order to reach an agreement," Annan said.
Fino failed in day-long talks on Monday to convince them to lift the boycott and warned of a growing crisis.

"Although the debate continued all Monday, it failed not only to bring compromise or come near to compromise, but on the contrary took Albania to the edge of a deeper crisis with unforeseen consequences," Fino's office said in a statement.
In an impasse, Fino late on Monday spoke with Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, European envoy Vranitzky and U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum.
"I told the parties I would not discuss with them any more but I will address international public opinion," Fino said.
Although Albania is calmer, lawlessness reigns in several areas and nine people have been killed in gunfire since Sunday.
Italy, leading a multinational force protecting humanitarian aid, called again for political compromise.
"The next 24 hours are very important for the future of Albania," Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta told reporters in Rome.
Prime Minister Prodi said he would work to the "last hours" to make sure elections go ahead.

Greece said failure to reach an election compromise would jeopardise the continued presence of the 6,000-strong eight-nation troop force. Western countries have already warned they may cut aid to Albania unless elections go ahead.
